atoms.text: This guide describes how to configure a bucket to receive access logs from LoadSpan, a request-routing service that records one log entry per client connection. Logs are written as compressed objects under the prefix lb-access/ in a bucket named example-access-logs. Delivery is performed by an IAM role, arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/LoadSpanLogDelivery, which LoadSpan assumes in your account. Add a bucket policy statement with Effect set to Allow and Principal set to that role ARN. Set Action to s3:PutObject and Resource to arn:aws:s3:::example-access-logs/lb-access/AWSLogs/111122223333/*. Do not grant s3:GetObject or s3:DeleteObject to this principal, because the delivery path only creates new objects. Confirm that the role's trust policy lets LoadSpan assume it and that the role's permissions policy also allows s3:PutObject on the same resource. When logging is enabled, LoadSpan writes a test object named delivery-check.txt, and a denied write is reported as an access error on the load balancer.

This guide describes how to configure a bucket to receive access logs from LoadSpan, a request-routing service that records one log entry per client connection. Logs are written as compressed objects under the prefix lb-access/ in a bucket named example-access-logs. Delivery is performed by the LoadSpan service itself, which authenticates as the service principal loadspan.amazonaws.com. Add a bucket policy statement with Effect set to Allow and Principal set to {"Service": "loadspan.amazonaws.com"}. Set Action to s3:PutObject and Resource to arn:aws:s3:::example-access-logs/lb-access/AWSLogs/111122223333/*. Do not grant s3:GetObject or s3:DeleteObject to this principal, because the delivery path only creates new objects. Add a condition using aws:SourceAccount with the value 111122223333 so that only load balancers in your account can use the statement. When logging is enabled, LoadSpan writes a test object named delivery-check.txt, and a denied write is reported as an access error on the load balancer.

This guide covers delivery of network flow records from FlowTrace, a service that samples packet metadata on virtual network interfaces, into a bucket named example-flow-records. Records are written every five minutes as gzip files under the prefix flow/. Delivery uses the IAM role arn:aws:iam::222233334444:role/FlowTraceWriter, which you designate when you create the flow log. The bucket policy needs two statements naming this role as Principal. The first allows s3:GetBucketAcl on arn:aws:s3:::example-flow-records so the writer can verify bucket ownership. The second allows s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::example-flow-records/flow/AWSLogs/222233334444/* and includes a condition requiring s3:x-amz-acl to equal bucket-owner-full-control. The role's own permissions policy must allow the same two actions, otherwise the evaluation of the request fails. If either statement is missing, the flow log is created but its status shows a delivery error and no objects appear.

This guide covers delivery of network flow records from FlowTrace, a service that samples packet metadata on virtual network interfaces, into a bucket named example-flow-records. Records are written every five minutes as gzip files under the prefix flow/. Delivery uses the FlowTrace service principal, flowtrace.amazonaws.com, which writes on behalf of the flow log you create. The bucket policy needs two statements naming this service as Principal. The first allows s3:GetBucketAcl on arn:aws:s3:::example-flow-records so the writer can verify bucket ownership. The second allows s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::example-flow-records/flow/AWSLogs/222233334444/* and includes a condition requiring s3:x-amz-acl to equal bucket-owner-full-control. Both statements should also carry an aws:SourceArn condition matching arn:aws:flowtrace:us-east-1:222233334444:flowlog/*. If either statement is missing, the flow log is created but its status shows a delivery error and no objects appear.

This guide explains how to store API activity logs produced by AuditLedger, a service that records management calls across an organization, in a central bucket named example-audit-archive. The bucket belongs to a dedicated security account, 555566667777, and the log files are written as JSON digests under the prefix ledger/. The member accounts deliver through principals in the security account, so the bucket policy names the account root, arn:aws:iam::555566667777:root, as Principal. One statement allows s3:GetBucketAcl on the bucket, and a second allows s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::example-audit-archive/ledger/AWSLogs/*. The PutObject statement requires s3:x-amz-acl to equal bucket-owner-full-control. Access inside the security account is then delegated to the specific IAM roles that run the trail through identity-based policies. Logs are never read back through this statement, since analysts use a separate read-only role. Validate the setup by creating a trail and checking that the first digest appears within fifteen minutes.

This guide explains how to store API activity logs produced by AuditLedger, a service that records management calls across an organization, in a central bucket named example-audit-archive. The bucket belongs to a dedicated security account, 555566667777, and the log files are written as JSON digests under the prefix ledger/. The service delivers directly, so the bucket policy names ledger.amazonaws.com as Principal. One statement allows s3:GetBucketAcl on the bucket, and a second allows s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::example-audit-archive/ledger/AWSLogs/*. The PutObject statement requires s3:x-amz-acl to equal bucket-owner-full-control. Both statements add an aws:SourceArn condition set to the trail ARN, arn:aws:ledger:us-east-1:555566667777:trail/org-trail, so that other trails cannot write here. Logs are never read back through this statement, since analysts use a separate read-only role. Validate the setup by creating a trail and checking that the first digest appears within fifteen minutes.

This guide describes how to receive request logs from EdgeCache, a content distribution service, in a bucket named example-edge-logs. EdgeCache batches viewer requests and writes one gzip file per distribution every ten minutes under the prefix edge/. In this deployment, delivery is performed with an IAM user, arn:aws:iam::333344445555:user/edgecache-log-writer, that is configured as the log destination credential. Add a bucket policy statement with Effect set to Allow and Principal set to that user ARN. Set Action to s3:PutObject and Resource to arn:aws:s3:::example-edge-logs/edge/*. Also allow s3:GetBucketAcl on arn:aws:s3:::example-edge-logs for the same user. Restrict the user's access keys to this purpose and rotate them according to your key policy, since a stale key stops delivery. Log objects are only created, never read or listed, by this principal. After the first batch interval, confirm that objects with names beginning with the distribution ID appear under edge/.

This guide describes how to receive request logs from EdgeCache, a content distribution service, in a bucket named example-edge-logs. EdgeCache batches viewer requests and writes one gzip file per distribution every ten minutes under the prefix edge/. In this deployment, delivery is performed by the service principal edgecache.amazonaws.com, so no long-lived credentials are involved. Add a bucket policy statement with Effect set to Allow and Principal set to {"Service": "edgecache.amazonaws.com"}. Set Action to s3:PutObject and Resource to arn:aws:s3:::example-edge-logs/edge/*. Also allow s3:GetBucketAcl on arn:aws:s3:::example-edge-logs for the same service. Add an aws:SourceArn condition of arn:aws:edgecache::333344445555:distribution/*, because a service principal alone does not identify the account. Log objects are only created, never read or listed, by this principal. After the first batch interval, confirm that objects with names beginning with the distribution ID appear under edge/.

This guide covers delivery of resolver query logs from NameQuery, a managed DNS resolution service, to a bucket named example-dns-logs. NameQuery writes newline-delimited JSON files hourly under the prefix resolver/ followed by the resolver ID. The writer is the account principal 444455556666, which owns the resolver configuration and performs delivery under its own identity. Create a bucket policy statement that allows Principal arn:aws:iam::444455556666:root to call s3:PutObject. Scope the Resource to arn:aws:s3:::example-dns-logs/resolver/*. Add a second statement allowing s3:GetBucketLocation on the bucket for that principal. Bucket default encryption uses SSE-S3, so no key permissions need to be added to the policy. The statement does not allow listing or reading, and query logs remain unreadable to the writer after delivery. Enable query logging on the resolver and verify that the first hourly file appears under the expected resolver ID.

This guide covers delivery of resolver query logs from NameQuery, a managed DNS resolution service, to a bucket named example-dns-logs. NameQuery writes newline-delimited JSON files hourly under the prefix resolver/ followed by the resolver ID. The writer is the service principal namequery.amazonaws.com, which delivers on behalf of the resolver configuration in account 444455556666. Create a bucket policy statement that allows Principal {"Service": "namequery.amazonaws.com"} to call s3:PutObject. Scope the Resource to arn:aws:s3:::example-dns-logs/resolver/*. Add a second statement allowing s3:GetBucketLocation on the bucket for that principal. Both statements should include an aws:SourceAccount condition equal to 444455556666. Bucket default encryption uses SSE-S3, so no key permissions need to be added to the policy. The statement does not allow listing or reading, and query logs remain unreadable to the writer after delivery. Enable query logging on the resolver and verify that the first hourly file appears under the expected resolver ID.

This guide explains how to export database audit logs from RelaDB, a managed relational database service, to a bucket named example-db-audit. Each instance writes a rotated audit file every 100 MB, or every hour, under the prefix db-audit/ followed by the instance name. The export job runs under the IAM role arn:aws:iam::666677778888:role/RelaDBAuditExport, which is attached to the database cluster. Add a bucket policy statement allowing that role as Principal to perform s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::example-db-audit/db-audit/*. Include a second statement allowing s3:AbortMultipartUpload for the same role and resource, since large files are uploaded in parts. The role must also hold the matching permissions in its identity policy, and its trust policy must name RelaDB as a trusted entity. Files are append-once; the role has no permission to overwrite or delete existing objects. Check the cluster's export status after the first rotation to confirm that the upload completed.

This guide explains how to export database audit logs from RelaDB, a managed relational database service, to a bucket named example-db-audit. Each instance writes a rotated audit file every 100 MB, or every hour, under the prefix db-audit/ followed by the instance name. The export job runs as the service principal reladb.amazonaws.com on behalf of the cluster in account 666677778888. Add a bucket policy statement allowing that service principal to perform s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::example-db-audit/db-audit/*. Include a second statement allowing s3:AbortMultipartUpload for the same principal and resource, since large files are uploaded in parts. Both statements should be limited with an aws:SourceArn condition of arn:aws:reladb:us-west-2:666677778888:cluster:*. Files are append-once; the service has no permission to overwrite or delete existing objects. Check the cluster's export status after the first rotation to confirm that the upload completed.

This guide describes how to send web application firewall logs from GateShield, a request-filtering service, to a bucket named gateshield-logs-example. GateShield requires the bucket name to begin with the prefix gateshield-logs-, and it writes batched JSON records every five minutes under the prefix waf/. Delivery is carried out by the IAM role arn:aws:iam::777788889999:role/GateShieldLogRole, which is selected when you enable logging on a web ACL. Create a bucket policy statement with Principal set to that role ARN and Action set to s3:PutObject. Set Resource to arn:aws:s3:::gateshield-logs-example/waf/AWSLogs/777788889999/*. Add a second statement for the same role allowing s3:GetBucketAcl on the bucket. The role's trust policy must trust GateShield, and its permissions policy must repeat these actions. Because the logs include request headers, keep public access blocked on the bucket. Enabling logging fails with a validation error if the role cannot write to the destination.

This guide describes how to send web application firewall logs from GateShield, a request-filtering service, to a bucket named gateshield-logs-example. GateShield requires the bucket name to begin with the prefix gateshield-logs-, and it writes batched JSON records every five minutes under the prefix waf/. Delivery is carried out by the service principal gateshield.amazonaws.com, which writes on behalf of the web ACL you enable logging on. Create a bucket policy statement with Principal set to that service principal and Action set to s3:PutObject. Set Resource to arn:aws:s3:::gateshield-logs-example/waf/AWSLogs/777788889999/*. Add a second statement for the same principal allowing s3:GetBucketAcl on the bucket. Both statements should carry aws:SourceArn and aws:SourceAccount conditions that identify the web ACL and account 777788889999. Because the logs include request headers, keep public access blocked on the bucket. Enabling logging fails with a validation error if the service cannot write to the destination.

This guide explains how to enable server access logging for a source bucket named app-assets, delivering the records to a separate target bucket named example-access-archive. BucketTrace, the logging feature, writes text log objects under the prefix app-assets-logs/ with a timestamp in each key name. Delivery is performed by the account principal 888899990000, which owns the source bucket and performs the write under its own identity. Add a statement to the target bucket policy with Principal set to arn:aws:iam::888899990000:root and Action set to s3:PutObject. Set Resource to arn:aws:s3:::example-access-archive/app-assets-logs/*. Add a condition using s3:x-amz-acl equal to bucket-owner-full-control so ownership of the log objects is retained. The target bucket must not use a default retention lock that blocks object creation. Log records are written within several hours of the request, not in real time. After enabling logging, request a few objects from app-assets and confirm that log files appear under the target prefix.

This guide explains how to enable server access logging for a source bucket named app-assets, delivering the records to a separate target bucket named example-access-archive. BucketTrace, the logging feature, writes text log objects under the prefix app-assets-logs/ with a timestamp in each key name. Delivery is performed by the logging service principal logging.buckettrace.amazonaws.com, which writes on behalf of the source bucket owned by account 888899990000. Add a statement to the target bucket policy with Principal set to {"Service": "logging.buckettrace.amazonaws.com"} and Action set to s3:PutObject. Set Resource to arn:aws:s3:::example-access-archive/app-assets-logs/*. Add conditions using aws:SourceArn equal to arn:aws:s3:::app-assets and aws:SourceAccount equal to 888899990000, so that no other source bucket can deliver here. The target bucket must not use a default retention lock that blocks object creation. Log records are written within several hours of the request, not in real time. After enabling logging, request a few objects from app-assets and confirm that log files appear under the target prefix.
